questions.qtext: Consider a system with a block size of $p$ words. What is the range of words present in the $\mathrm{k^{th}}$ block of main memory?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

The correct answer is A. $k \cdot p \text{ to } (k+1) \cdot p - 1$.

Here is the step-by-step derivation:

1. Understanding Block Organization

Main memory is essentially a long list of words addressed linearly: $0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$

This memory is divided into fixed-size chunks called blocks.

  • Block Size ($p$): This means every block holds exactly $p$ words.

  • Block Index ($k$): We assume standard 0-based indexing where the first block is Block 0, the second is Block 1, and so on.

2. Deriving the Start Address

To find the starting word of Block $k$, we just need to count how many words are contained in all the blocks that come before it.

  • Before Block $k$, there are exactly $k$ blocks (Block $0$ to Block $k-1$).

  • Since each block has $p$ words, the total words before Block $k$ is $k \times p$.

  • Therefore, the first word of Block $k$ starts at address:

    $$\text{Start Address} = k \cdot p$$

3. Deriving the End Address

Since the block contains $p$ words, the addresses range from the start address to Start + p - 1.

  • $\text{End Address} = \text{Start Address} + (p - 1)$

  • $\text{End Address} = k \cdot p + p - 1$

  • Factoring out $p$, we get:

    $$\text{End Address} = (k + 1) \cdot p - 1$$

Example Verification

Let's assume the block size is 4 words ($p = 4$).

  • Block 0 ($k=0$): Contains words 0, 1, 2, 3.

    • Formula A: $0 \cdot 4$ to $(1) \cdot 4 - 1 \Rightarrow 0 \text{ to } 3$. (Correct)

  • Block 1 ($k=1$): Contains words 4, 5, 6, 7.

    • Formula A: $1 \cdot 4$ to $(2) \cdot 4 - 1 \Rightarrow 4 \text{ to } 7$. (Correct)

  • Block 2 ($k=2$): Contains words 8, 9, 10, 11.

    • Formula A: $2 \cdot 4$ to $(3) \cdot 4 - 1 \Rightarrow 8 \text{ to } 11$. (Correct)

Why other options are wrong:

  • B: Uses $p^2$, which would imply the block size grows quadratically, which is incorrect.

  • C: Uses $2^p$. This would be correct only if $p$ was defined as the number of offset bits (meaning block size is $2^p$). But the problem explicitly states the block size is $p$ words.

  • D: Also uses $2^p$, making it incorrect for the same reason as C.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Block numbers start from $0$.

Analogy to $0$-indexing in an Array:

  • $0^{\text{th}}$ has $0$ elements before it

  • $1^{\text{st}}$ has $1$ element before it

  • $2^{\text{nd}}$ has $2$ elements before it

  • $\vdots$

  • $i^{\text{th}}$ has $i$ elements before it

Similarly, in this question:

  • $k^{\text{th}}$ block has $k$ blocks before it $\implies k \cdot p$ words before it

  • $(k+1)^{\text{th}}$ block has $k+1$ blocks before it $\implies (k+1) \cdot p$ words before it

Thus, the range of words in the $k^{\text{th}}$ block is:

$$k \cdot p \text{ to } (k+1) \cdot p - 1$$

Answer: (A)

questions.qtext:
Consider a small two-way set-associative cache memory, consisting of four blocks. For choosing the block to be replaced, use the least recently used (LRU) scheme. The number of cache misses for the following sequence of block addresses is:

$$8, 12, 0, 12, 8$$
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/nUPpGN3nd5Y

$8$ - Compulsory/Cold Miss

$12$ - Compulsory/Cold Miss

$0$ - Compulsory/Cold Miss

$12$ - Hit

$8$ - Conflict Miss

We have $4$ blocks and $2$ blocks in a set

$\implies$ there are $2$ sets. So blocks will go to sets as follows:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf {Set Number} & \textbf{Block Number} \\\hline \text{0} & \text{0,8,12} \\\hline\text{1} & \\\hline \end{array}$$
Since the lowest bit of block address is used for indexing into the set, so $8, 12$ and $0$ first miss in cache with $0$ replacing $8$ (there are two slots in each set due to $2-\text{way}$ set) and then $12$ hits in cache and $8$ again misses. So, totally $4$ misses.

Correct Answer: $C$
